The advancement of intelligent road transport represents a promising direction in the evolution of transportation systems, aimed at improving road safety and reducing traffic accidents. The integration of artificial intelligence, sensors, and machine vision systems enables autonomous vehicles (AVs) to rapidly adapt to changes in the road environment, minimizing human error and significantly reducing collision risks. Connected vehicles utilizing C-V2X (Cellular Vehicle-to-Everything) communication primarily feature real-time operation, safety, and stability. However, communication flaws, such as signal fading, time delays, packet loss, and malicious network attacks, can affect vehicle-to-vehicle interactions in cooperative intelligent transport systems (C-ITSs). This study explores how C-V2X technology, compared to traditional DSRC, improves communication latency and enhances vehicle communication efficiency. Using SUMO simulations, various traffic scenarios were modeled with different autonomous vehicle penetration rates and communication technologies, focusing on traffic conflict rates, travel time, and communication performance. The results demonstrated that C-V2X reduced latency by over 99% compared to DSRC, facilitating faster communication between vehicles and contributing to a 38% reduction in traffic conflicts at 60% AV penetration. While C-V2X offers substantial benefits, challenges such as data packet loss, communication delays, and security vulnerabilities must be addressed to fully realize its potential. Future advancements in 5G and subsequent wireless communication technologies are expected to further reduce latency and enhance the effectiveness of C-ITSs. This study underscores the potential of C-V2X to enhance collision avoidance, alleviate congestion, and improve traffic management, while also contributing to the development of more reliable and efficient transportation systems. Moreover, multiple network access points are deployed as road equipments in the form of Road-Side Units (RSUs), and diverse vehicles roam the playground, including an autonomous shuttle, along with connected delivery robots, as well as non-autonomous vehicles. These vehicles are given the ability to communicate via their On-Board Unit (OBU), an embedded equipment containing interfaces for each dedicated vehicular Radio Access Technology (RAT), as well as commercial cellular networks like LTE and 5G Non-Standalone (NSA). Moreover, an experimental 5G Standalone (SA) network, with its dedicated access point (AP) and core, is scheduled for deployment in the near future, providing an extra possibility for high-performance communications. Moreover, relaying can also intervene as a connectivity solution in situations where D2D communication between source and destination is disturbed or low-performance, such as Non Line of Sight (NLOS) situations.
